text: GPGPU is {{c1::heterogeneous}} computing. The {{c2::CPU}} host runs the main program, and the kernels run on the {{c3::GPU}} device.
extra: The host loads the data, copies it to the device, launches the kernel, then copies the results back.

text: The CPU and GPU usually have {{c1::separate}} memory. Getting data onto the GPU means a slow {{c2::copy}} over the bus, and on a small problem that copy can take longer than the compute it saves.
extra: So a straight GPU port of a small job can run slower than plain CPU code.

text: To get good GPU performance from Warp, use {{c1::flat, contiguous}} buffers, give each thread the {{c2::same}} amount of work, and keep CPU to GPU copies to a minimum.
extra: Branches that send threads down different paths and scattered data both slow down GPU threads that run in lockstep.

text: A function marked {{c1::@wp.kernel}} is statically typed, and it {{c2::cannot return}} a value. It writes its result into an output array instead.
extra: You write the body for one element. Warp runs one thread per element.

text: Inside a Warp kernel, {{c1::wp.tid()}} gives each thread its own element index. So the add kernel writes z[tid] = x[tid] + y[tid].
extra: It plays the same role as a thread ID in Pthreads or a rank in MPI.

text: A kernel thread can read any input element, but its output must {{c1::not depend on another thread's output}}. That independence is what lets the GPU run every thread at once.
extra: Each thread writes exactly one output slot.

text: You want a kernel over \(N\) elements on an Nvidia GPU. You call wp.launch with the kernel, {{c1::dim=N}}, the arguments in order in {{c2::inputs=}}, and {{c3::device="cuda"}}.
extra: This is study guide practice question 3, answer C. The device argument is optional and falls back to Warp's default device.

text: With device="cpu", Warp runs the kernel as {{c1::serial}} code for portability. With device="cuda", it runs {{c2::in parallel}} on an Nvidia GPU.
extra: The code is the same on both. CPU mode lets you test without a GPU, but you get no speedup.

text: On the host you wrap a NumPy array with {{c1::wp.array}}, allocate the output with {{c2::wp.zeros}}, and after the launch call {{c3::.numpy()}} to get the results back.
extra: Match the dtype and the device on every array you pass in.
